doc_description: Costco Wholesale Corporation’s Form 10-K (Annual Report) for the fiscal year ended August 29, 2021 (NASDAQ: COST) details its global membership-warehouse operations (815 warehouses across 12 countries), 2021 performance ($195.9B revenue; $5.0B net income), comprehensive risk factors and MD&A, KPMG unqualified audit opinions and effective controls, property footprint, shareholder matters, and full exhibits/signatures.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC filing: Costco Wholesale Corporation Form 10-K (Annual Report) for fiscal year ended August 29, 2021; Commission File No. 0-20355.
- Company details: Incorporated in Washington; IRS EIN 91-1223280; principal offices at 999 Lake Drive, Issaquah, WA 98027; phone (425) 313-8100.
- Securities: Common Stock, $.01 par value, ticker COST, listed on The NASDAQ Global Select Market; no securities registered under Section 12(g).
- Registrant status/checkmarks: Well-known seasoned issuer; required to file and has filed all required reports; submitted all Interactive Data Files; large accelerated filer; not an accelerated, non-accelerated, smaller reporting, or emerging growth company; auditor attestation on internal control over financial reporting under SOX 404(b); not a shell company.
- Market and share data: Aggregate market value of voting stock held by non-affiliates as of February 14, 2021: $155,810,963,274; shares outstanding as of September 28, 2021: 441,823,811.
- Incorporation by reference: Portions of Proxy Statement for the January 20, 2022 Annual Meeting incorporated into Part III.
- Table of Contents highlights:
  - Part I: Business; Risk Factors; Unresolved Staff Comments; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Mine Safety Disclosures.
  - Part II: Market for Common Equity and related matters; MD&A; Market Risk Disclosures; Financial Statements and Supplementary Data; Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants; Controls and Procedures; Other Information.
  - Part III: Directors, Executive Officers and Corporate Governance; Executive Compensation; Security Ownership and related matters; Certain Relationships and Related Transactions, and Director Independence; Principal Accounting Fees and Services.
  - Part IV: Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedules; Form 10-K Summary; Signatures.

structure.heading: PART I
structure.start_phrase: Costco Wholesale Corporation and its subsidiaries (Costco or the Company) began operations in 1983, in Seattle, Washington.
structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements caution: The report includes statements about future expectations (e.g., sales growth, comparable sales, warehouse openings/closures, pricing, EPS, stock-based compensation, capex, accounting standards, financing, margins, ROIC, strategy, expense control, membership renewal, shopping frequency, litigation, product/service demand). Such statements are identifiable by terms like “anticipate,” “expect,” etc., are subject to risks outlined in Item 1A (Risk Factors), Item 7 (MD&A), and Item 8 (financials), and are not updated except as required by law.
- Company overview: Costco Wholesale Corporation, founded in 1983 in Seattle, operates membership warehouses in the U.S. and Puerto Rico, Canada, U.K., Mexico, Japan, Korea, Australia, Spain, France, Iceland, China, and via a majority-owned subsidiary in Taiwan.
- Scale: 815 warehouses at August 29, 2021; 795 at August 30, 2020; 782 at September 1, 2019.
- E-commerce presence: Websites in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, U.K., Korea, Taiwan, Japan, and Australia.
- Public listing: Common stock trades on NASDAQ Global Select Market under the ticker “COST.”
- Fiscal calendar: 52/53-week year ending the Sunday nearest end of August; 13 four-week periods (with an extra week in the 53rd week); first three quarters have three periods each, fourth has four; references to 2021, 2020, 2019 correspond to fiscal years ended Aug 29, 2021; Aug 30, 2020; Sept 1, 2019.
- Seasonality: Higher net sales and earnings during the winter holiday season.
- Business model: Offer low prices on a limited selection of national brands and private-label products across categories to drive high sales volumes and rapid inventory turnover.
- Operating approach: Profitability achieved with significantly lower gross margins than most retailers through volume purchasing, efficient distribution, reduced merchandise handling, and no-frills, self-service warehouses.
- Working capital discipline: Generally sell inventory before payment is due to suppliers, while taking advantage of early payment discounts.
- Supply chain and distribution: Predominantly purchase directly from manufacturers; use cross-docking depots to consolidate large shipments and quickly ship to warehouses, creating freight and handling efficiencies and lowering costs compared to traditional multi-step channels.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: Costco Wholesale Corporation and its subsidiaries (Costco or the Company) began operations in 1983, in Seattle, Washington.
structure.summary:
- Cautionary statement on forward‑looking statements, referencing applicable securities laws and noting risks outlined in Risk Factors, MD&A, and financial statements.
- Item 1—Business: Overview of Costco’s membership‑warehouse model, global footprint, e‑commerce presence, NASDAQ listing (COST), 52/53‑week fiscal year, and seasonality.
- Operating model and logistics: Limited‑SKU, low‑margin/high‑volume strategy; direct sourcing; cross‑dock depots; e‑commerce fulfillment via depots, logistics for bulky items, and drop‑ship; warehouse design, average size (~146k sq. ft.), hours, shrinkage controls, accepted payment methods; return and warranty policies.
- Merchandise and services: Core categories (Foods & Sundries, Non‑Foods, Fresh Foods); Warehouse Ancillary (gas, pharmacy, optical, food court, hearing aids, tire) and Other Businesses (e‑commerce, business centers, Costco Travel). Gas represented ~9% of 2021 net sales; e‑commerce ~7%.
- Supply chain and private label: Diversified suppliers, COVID‑19 supply disruptions and mitigation; emphasis on private‑label (Kirkland Signature) for value and margin; intent to grow private‑label penetration.
- Membership: Gold Star and Business tiers, $60 annual fee in U.S./Canada, household cards, worldwide use; renewal rates (91% U.S./Canada; 89% worldwide in 2021); standardized counting methodology; member counts (2019–2021); Executive membership upgrade ($60 in U.S./Canada), 2% reward (cap $1,000), added services, and higher spend/visit behavior; Executive penetration stats by region.
- Human capital: 288,000 employees in 2021 (regional breakdown provided), focus on competitive pay/benefits, promote‑from‑within, majority full‑time workforce, high retention (>90% after 1 year in U.S.); DEI initiatives; COVID‑19 responses (premium pay through Feb 2021; added PTO for childcare); reference to sustainability reporting.
- Competition: Highly competitive retail landscape across formats (supermarkets, supercenters, e‑commerce, discounters, specialty, gasoline); key U.S. competitors include Walmart, Target, Kroger, Amazon; warehouse clubs Sam’s Club and BJ’s.
- Intellectual property: Importance of trademarks and Kirkland Signature brand; protection strategies; ongoing plan to expand private‑label sales.
- Investor information and governance: Website access to SEC filings; code of ethics for senior financial officers; disclosure practices for amendments/waivers.
- Executive officers: Listing of senior leadership with roles, tenure, and ages; each has 25+ years of company service.
- Item 1A—Risk Factors (partial): Heavy dependence on U.S./Canada (notably California) performance; risks from comps, cost pressures, store openings/cannibalization, mix shifts, and macro conditions; challenges executing growth (site acquisition, permitting, regulations, community opposition, lease terms); risks of expanding in existing/new markets (cannibalization, competition, local preferences, seasonality); no assurance new warehouses or e‑commerce sites will be profitable.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: The risks described below could materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Excerpt from a public company’s annual report (Item 1A—Risk Factors through Item 4), detailing operational, market, legal/regulatory risks, and property footprint.
- Business and operating risks:
  - Heavy dependence on U.S. and Canada, especially California; adverse local trends could materially impact results.
  - Growth execution risks: site acquisition and leasing constraints, community and regulatory opposition, large‐retailer restrictions, cannibalization in existing markets, unfamiliarity in new markets/e-commerce profitability, and uncertain returns from supply chain/delivery investments and acquisitions.
  - Membership model risks: maintaining growth, renewals, brand trust; specific reliance on Kirkland Signature quality, pricing, and availability.
  - Operational disruptions: distribution, processing, packaging, and manufacturing interruptions; third-party logistics dependencies for e-commerce.
  - Merchandising and demand: failure to anticipate consumer and ESG-driven preferences, leading to excess inventory or stockouts.
  - Technology: critical IT system availability and large transformation projects; need for digital resiliency against outages and disasters.
  - Cybersecurity and privacy: growing, sophisticated threats; third-party/vendor risks; potential legal exposure under GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA; insurance/indemnity may be insufficient.
  - Payments: dependency on processors, interchange costs, evolving network rules, PCI DSS compliance, and potential fraud/liability.
  - Product safety: risk of illness/injury, recalls, litigation, and reputational harm across food, drugs, children’s, pet, and durable goods.
  - Omnichannel execution: need to meet rising digital expectations across web and mobile.
  - Talent: attracting, training, and retaining employees and leadership; labor and benefits cost pressures.
  - Insurance/self-insurance exposure: potential uncovered or catastrophic property and business interruption losses.
- Market and external risks:
  - Intense competition across retail formats and online channels; price transparency heightens pressure.
  - Macroeconomic volatility: energy/fuel costs, inflation, unemployment, FX, tariffs/trade policy (notably U.S., China, U.K.), commodity price swings, geopolitical events.
  - Supply chain and supplier risks: availability, pricing, quality/compliance lapses, and disruptions.
  - Foreign exchange: translation and purchasing currency impacts, growing international exposure.
  - Catastrophic events: natural disasters, extreme weather, terrorism/violence, energy shortages, public health emergencies disrupting operations and demand.
  - COVID-19: continuing uncertainty affecting demand, inventory, fulfillment, costs, labor availability, supply chains, litigation exposure, and financial markets; potential to amplify other risks.
  - Climate change: regulatory costs (GHG), physical risks to supply and operations, and demand shifts (e.g., gasoline).
  - Market expectations: risk of stock price decline if key metrics underperform.
- Legal and regulatory risks:
  - International operations: political/economic instability, regulatory regimes, trade sanctions/tariffs, currency controls, Brexit impacts, tax and IP challenges, and management complexity.
  - Accounting: changes in standards and management estimates could materially affect reported results.
  - Internal controls: SOX 404 compliance risks could impair reporting and investor confidence.
  - Taxes: changing laws/rates, audits (including transfer pricing), and non-income tax exposures could increase liabilities.
  - Environmental/health/safety: extensive regulations on hazardous materials, waste, refrigeration, wastewater; noncompliance could lead to fines, shutdowns, or liabilities.
  - Legal proceedings and audits: potential for significant costs, operational constraints, and management distraction.
- Properties (as of August 29, 2021):
  - 815 warehouses (U.S. & Puerto Rico 564; Canada 105; Other International 146); mix of owned and leased sites (many land-only leases).
  - Approx. 118.9 million sq ft of warehouse space (83.2M U.S.; 14.9M Canada; 20.8M Other International) and 31.4 million sq ft of distribution/logistics facilities.
  - Additional processing, packaging, manufacturing, and other facilities, including private-label production.
- Other disclosures:
  - Item 1B—Unresolved Staff Comments: None.
  - Item 3—Legal Proceedings: Referenced to financial statement note.
  - Item 4—Mine Safety Disclosures: Not applicable.

- Item 7—Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A):
  - Scope and structure: MD&A is a supplement to the consolidated financial statements; focuses on 2021 vs. 2020, with 2020 vs. 2019 discussion referenced in the FY2020 Form 10-K. In 2021, hardlines and softlines were combined into “non-foods” (no material impact on results discussion).
  - Key profitability driver: Increasing net sales, especially comparable sales growth, to leverage SG&A.
  - Net sales components: Core merchandise (foods and sundries, non-foods, fresh foods), warehouse ancillary businesses (gasoline, pharmacy, optical, food court, hearing aids, tire installation), and other businesses (e-commerce, business centers, travel, other).
  - Comparable sales definition: Warehouses and e-commerce sites operating more than one year, including remodels/relocations/expansions.
  - External factors: Currency exchange rates, gasoline prices, and competitive dynamics can significantly influence sales and margins.
  - Strategy and pricing philosophy: Maintain “pricing authority” by offering quality at competitive prices; may reduce or hold prices despite cost increases, which can compress gross margin percentage; expand private-label penetration and online offerings to adapt to market conditions.
  - Gasoline business dynamics: Draws members; lower gross margin percentage but lower SG&A as a percent of sales; rising gas prices typically boost net sales and lower SG&A as a percent of sales but compress gross margin percentage, with the inverse effect when prices decline.

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
The following Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations (MD&A) is intended to promote
understanding of the results of operations and financial condition.
structure.summary:
- Scope and framing
  - Management’s Discussion and Analysis for fiscal 2021 vs. 2020; 2020 vs. 2019 referenced to prior 10-K.
  - Fiscal year ends Sunday closest to August 31; 2021, 2020, and 2019 were 52-week years.
  - Hardlines and softlines combined into “non-foods” in 2021.

- Business model and key profitability drivers
  - Focus on net sales growth, especially comparable sales (defined for warehouses and e-commerce >1 year).
  - Major external influences: foreign exchange, gasoline prices, competition, tariffs, inflation/deflation.
  - Pricing philosophy prioritizes member value and “pricing authority,” which can pressure gross margin.
  - Gasoline and e-commerce typically carry lower gross margin percentages; gas lowers SG&A as a percent of sales.
  - Membership model central to profitability (renewals, Executive memberships).
  - Cost control emphasis, with competitive employee compensation; low-margin model magnifies small cost changes.
  - International operations share model but differ in growth rates, cost structures, competition, and e-commerce presence.
  - Methodologies for isolating FX and gasoline impacts on results are described.

- 2021 highlights
  - Opened 22 warehouses (including 2 relocations): U.S. +12 net, Canada +4 net, Other International +4.
  - Net sales up 18% to $192,052; comparable sales up 16%.
  - Membership fee revenue up 9% to $3,877.
  - Gross margin percentage down 7 bps; SG&A as % of sales down 40 bps.
  - Effective tax rate 24.0% (24.4% in 2020).
  - Net income up 25% to $5,007 ($11.27 diluted EPS vs. $9.02).
  - Special cash dividend $10/share in Dec 2020; quarterly dividend increased to $0.79 in April 2021; total dividends $5,748.

- COVID-19 impacts
  - Sales mix moved toward pre-pandemic patterns; ancillary and other businesses rebounded.
  - Ongoing supply and logistics constraints expected to persist.
  - Paid $515 in incremental COVID-related wages in 2021 ($825 total from Mar 1, 2020–Feb 28, 2021).
  - Permanent wage increases effective March 1, 2021 (~$400 pre-tax annualized cost); possible added costs from local hazard pay mandates.

- Results of operations
  - Net sales: +$28,832 (+18%) driven by +16% comps and contributions from new warehouses; strength in non-foods, e-commerce, and gasoline.
    - FX tailwind +$2,759 (169 bps); gasoline price tailwind +$1,636 (100 bps); gasoline volume +10% (+$1,469; 90 bps).
  - Comparable sales: +16% total; e-commerce comps +44% (first half +80%).
    - Ex-FX and gasoline: U.S. +14%, Canada +12%, Other International +13%, Total +13%.
  - Membership fees: $3,877 (+9%); renewal rates 91% U.S./Canada and 89% worldwide; recognized ratably.
  - Gross margin: 11.13% (down 7 bps). Core merchandise margin (as % of core sales) up 23 bps; ex-gas inflation, GM% 11.22% (+2 bps).
    - Positives: non-foods, e-commerce, absence of prior-year inventory reserve.
    - Negatives: increased 2% rewards (-3 bps), LIFO charge (-2 bps). FX benefit ~$301.
    - Segment GM% ex-gas: down in U.S.; up in Canada and Other International.
  - SG&A: $18,461; 9.61% of net sales (down 40 bps; ex-gas 9.69%, down 32 bps).
    - Drivers: sales leverage in warehouse/other businesses (-24 bps), lower COVID wages (-8), lower central ops (-5), lower stock comp (-3), lower Innovel-related costs (-1).
    - Offsets: prior-year product tax assessment reversal effect (+5), IT asset write-off (+4). FX increased SG&A by ~$228.
  - Preopening: $76; 22 openings (U.S. 13, Canada 5, Other International 4, incl. relocations).
  - Interest expense: $171 (primarily Senior Notes).
  - Interest income and other, net: $143 (lower rates reduced interest income; higher FX transaction gains; 2020 included $36 debt repayment charge).
  - Income taxes: $1,601; effective rate 24.0%; discrete net tax benefits $163 (stock comp $75; special dividend via 401(k) $70; valuation allowance reduction $19). Excluding discrete, tax rate 26.4%.

- Liquidity and capital resources
  - Cash flows (2021): operating +$8,958; investing -$3,535; financing -$6,488.
  - Cash and cash equivalents + short-term investments: $12,175 (incl. unsettled card receivables $1,816).
  - Capital expenditures: $3,588 in 2021; plan $3,800–$4,200 for 2022; plan up to 35 new warehouses (incl. 5 relocations); COVID-related real estate/construction delays possible.
  - Stock repurchases: 1.358 million shares for ~$495 (avg $364.39); remaining authorization $3,250.
  - Dividends: $12.98/share in 2021, including $10 special ($4,430 aggregate); quarterly raised to $0.79.
  - Bank credit facilities: $1,050 total capacity (international $574, $201 guaranteed); letters of credit $235 total, $197 outstanding; short-term borrowings immaterial.
  - No material off-balance sheet arrangements.
  - Management expects existing liquidity and cash flows to meet foreseeable needs.

- Critical accounting estimates
  - Insurance/self-insurance liabilities for health care, workers’ compensation, general liability, property, D&O, vehicle, inventory loss, and other risks.
  - Estimates based on historical experience and actuarial assumptions; exposures partly reinsured; actual outcomes may vary but past adjustments not material.

- Market risk disclosures (Item 7A)
  - Interest rate risk: conservative investment policy in cash equivalents and short-term government/agency securities; 100 bps rate change would have immaterial fair value impact; fixed-rate long-term debt $7,531.
  - Foreign currency risk: use of forward foreign-exchange contracts to economically hedge non-functional currency exposures (primarily U.S. dollar inventory for international subsidiaries); hypothetical 10% strengthening of functional currency would reduce contract fair value by $149 and produce an unrealized loss of same amount.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase: Our exposure to financial market risk results from fluctuations in interest rates and foreign currency exchange rates.
structure.summary:
- Item 7A — Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk:
  - Overall policy: Exposure to interest rate and foreign currency risks; no speculative or trading activities.
  - Interest rate risk: Investment portfolio focused on principal preservation and yield; holdings in cash equivalents and short-term U.S. government/agency securities (3 months to 5 years), with strict investment limits by region (U.S., captive insurance, Canada/International). A 100 bp rate change at 2021 year-end would have had an immaterial impact on fair value; AFS unrealized gains/losses recorded in AOCI. Fixed-rate long-term debt totaled $7,531 at 2021 year-end; rate changes affect its fair value.
  - Foreign currency risk: Non-functional currency transactions at foreign subsidiaries hedged with forward FX contracts, primarily for U.S. dollar inventory purchases by non-U.S.-dollar functional subsidiaries; no speculation. A hypothetical 10% strengthening of functional currencies as of August 29, 2021 would decrease the contracts’ fair value by $149, creating an equivalent unrealized loss in income.
  - Commodity price risk: Exposure to electricity, natural gas, and fuel; partially mitigated through fixed-price contracts (mainly U.S. and Canada) and some index-based variable contracts. These generally qualify for the “normal purchases and normal sales” exception; no mark-to-market required.

- Item 8 — Financial Statements and Supplementary Data:
  - Independent auditor’s report for Costco Wholesale Corporation: Unqualified opinion that the consolidated financial statements present fairly the Company’s financial position as of August 29, 2021 and August 30, 2020, and results and cash flows for the 52-week periods ended August 29, 2021, August 30, 2020, and September 1, 2019, in conformity with U.S. GAAP.
  - Internal control over financial reporting: Unqualified opinion on effectiveness as of August 29, 2021 (COSO 2013).
  - Change in accounting principle: Adoption of ASC 842 (Leases) as of September 2, 2019.
  - Basis for opinion: PCAOB standards, independence, risk-based audit procedures, evaluation of estimates and presentation.
  - Critical audit matter: A CAM was identified and communicated (details not included in the excerpt).

structure.title: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.heading: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.start_phrase: We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheets of Costco Wholesale Corporation and subsidiaries (the Company) as of August 29, 2021 and August 30, 2020, the related consolidated statements of income, comprehensive income, equity, and cash flows for the 52- week periods ended August 29, 2021, August 30, 2020 and September 1, 2019, and the related notes (collectively, the consolidated financial statements).
structure.summary:
- Independent auditor’s reports (KPMG): unqualified opinions on Costco’s consolidated financial statements (fiscal 2019–2021) and on internal control over financial reporting as of August 29, 2021; noted adoption of ASC 842 (leases) in 2019; critical audit matter focused on estimating U.S. workers’ compensation self‑insurance liabilities.
- Consolidated financial statements presented:
  - Income: FY2021 total revenue $195.9B (net sales $192.1B; membership fees $3.88B), net income attributable to Costco $5.01B, diluted EPS $11.27.
  - Comprehensive income, statements of equity (including dividends and buybacks), and cash flows (FY2021 operating cash flow $9.0B; investing driven by $3.6B capex; financing included $5.7B dividends and share repurchases).
  - Balance sheet highlights at 8/29/21: assets $59.3B; liabilities $41.2B; total equity $18.1B; cash and equivalents $11.3B; inventories $14.2B.
- Significant accounting policies and related disclosures:
  - Business model, consolidation, fiscal year, use of estimates (including COVID-19 considerations).
  - Cash equivalents and credit/debit card receivables; short-term investments (AFS and HTM) and fair value hierarchy.
  - Receivables composition and credit loss allowances; inventories (U.S. LIFO, Canada/Other FIFO/retail), shrink and vendor rebates.
  - Property and equipment detail, depreciation, impairment approach; 2021 write-off of certain IT assets ($84).
  - Lease accounting under ASC 842 (ROU assets and liabilities; discount rates; expense components).
  - Goodwill/intangibles and annual impairment testing; goodwill balance ~$996M (includes Innovel/CWL).
  - Insurance/self-insurance programs and actuarial estimation; total self-insurance liabilities $1.257B.
  - Derivatives for FX exposures (forward contracts) and commodity purchase practices.
  - Foreign currency translation and transaction gains/losses.
  - Revenue recognition: point-of-sale and e-commerce timing; deferred membership fees ($2.042B); Executive 2% reward accounted as sales reduction ($2.047B in 2021); shop card breakage; co‑brand credit card economics.
  - Merchandise costs and vendor consideration; SG&A components; retirement plans; stock-based compensation (RSUs, vesting, expense recognition); preopening; income taxes; EPS; stock repurchases.
- Acquisition: Innovel Solutions (now Costco Wholesale Logistics) acquired in March 2020 for $999M; goodwill ~$940M (tax-deductible); strategic rationale in last‑mile capabilities.
- Investments and fair value: composition (U.S. government/agency securities, CDs), maturities, and Level 2 fair value measurements; derivative fair values disclosed.
- Debt: short-term facilities and borrowings; long-term Senior Notes (including 2020 issuances); carrying value ~$7.53B; maturity schedule; fair value estimates.
- Leases: balances for operating and finance leases, weighted-average terms/rates, expense detail, cash flows, and future minimum payments.
- Equity: dividends (including a $10.00 per share special dividend in 2021; current quarterly $0.79); share repurchase authorization of $4.0B (remaining $3.25B at FY2021) and annual activity.
- Stock-based compensation: RSU plan mechanics, 2021 grant/vesting/forfeiture activity, special dividend anti-dilution adjustment, expense ($665M), and remaining unrecognized cost and amortization period.
- Income taxes: pre-tax income by geography; total provision $1.601B; effective rate ~24%; deferred tax assets/liabilities (including lease-related amounts and valuation allowance for foreign tax credits); unrecognized tax benefits and audit status; other non‑income tax matters.
- Net income per share: basic and diluted share counts and methodology.
- Commitments and contingencies: overview of legal proceedings (labor and wage cases, opioid MDL participation, securities/derivative actions resolved, ERISA 401(k) case), with no expected material adverse effect on financials.
- Segment reporting: three reportable segments (U.S., Canada, Other International) with revenue, operating income, assets, capex, and depreciation by segment; disaggregated net sales by category (Foods & Sundries, Non‑Foods, Fresh Foods, Warehouse Ancillary & Other).
- Controls and procedures: no changes/disagreements with accountants; effective disclosure controls; management’s report on effective ICFR; no material changes in ICFR in the fourth quarter.
